title: SYSK Selects:  What's the deal with Voodoo?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of the July 2010-era episode "What's the Deal with Voodoo?" Josh and Chuck explain voodoo as a real religion rather than pop-culture caricature. They cover the 1791 Bois Caiman ceremony and Haitian Revolution, the supreme god Bondye and the loa (spirits, often tied to ancestors), the African roots in Ghana, Benin and Togo, and the Haitian form's syncretism with Catholicism. Other topics include spirit possession (horse and rider), papa Legba, animal sacrifice, bo versus voodoo, who-do in New Orleans, the Marie Laveau lineage, Western misconceptions and health concerns, and pop culture (Angel Heart, Serpent and the Rainbow, Live and Let Die). The episode closes with listener mail about Guantanamo detainee torture and a call for voodoo practitioners to write in.

segments.title: Selects intro and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces this Saturday Selects pick, 'What's the Deal with Voodoo?', and he and Chuck banter about Chuck's chair before going back in time.

segments.title: 1791 Haitian slave uprising and voodoo ceremony
segments.summary: The hosts describe a August ceremony in the Alligator Woods (Bois Caiman) where rebel leaders pledged to rebellion, followed by the slave uprising in Haiti that the hosts say led to a free republic by 1804. They note that voodoo's bad reputation among whites stems partly from these events, and that Pat Robertson's claim that Haiti made a pact with the devil is discussed.

segments.title: Voodoo as a religion: supreme god, loa, and ancestors
segments.summary: Voodoo is described as an actual religion with no definitive holy text, a supreme god (Bondye) reached through intermediary spirits called loa, which are based on ancestral spirits. The hosts compare the loa to pagan gods but say practitioners do not regard them as gods. Voodoo is described as mainly used for good, with evil magic called bo practiced in African tradition by some.

segments.title: African origins and spirit possession
segments.summary: The hosts trace the word voodoo to the Fon language of the kingdom of Fon in West Africa, meaning sacred spirit. They note roughly thirty million practitioners in Togo, Ghana and Benin, and that voodoo is an official religion in Benin. Spirit possession, where a loa rides a 'horse' (the possessed person), is identified as a central tenet.

segments.title: Haitian voodoo, papa Legba and Catholic syncretism
segments.summary: Haitian voodoo is described as creolized African voodoo, mixed with Catholicism after enslaved people were forced to convert under the Code Noir. Papa Legba, the gatekeeper between worlds, is invoked at ceremonies, and loa are matched to Catholic saints such as St. Peter, St. James and St. Patrick.

segments.title: Animal sacrifice, rituals, and possession dances
segments.summary: The hosts describe animal sacrifice to appease spirits, where an animal that refuses food is released and one that eats is killed quickly. Blood is mixed with rum, syrup and salt and shared. They also describe the Dance of the Hooded Gun, the belief that touching a possessed dancer is deadly, and the claim that the possessed feel no pain, citing a witnessed ritual.

segments.title: Western misconceptions, New Orleans, and pop culture
segments.summary: The hosts explain why Westerners fear voodoo, citing blood, death and spirits among the living. They describe the 1915-1935 US Marine occupation of Haiti and related books and films, the Marie Laveau lineage in New Orleans, and the emergence of hoodoo/who-do from the factions. They discuss the 1983 paper on zombies and HIV transmission, and public health concerns about shared blood and folk medicine. Movies Angel Heart, Serpent and the Rainbow and Live and Let Die are mentioned.

segments.title: Comparisons to Buddhism and Christianity
segments.summary: The hosts argue voodoo is not so different from other religions, noting that the Dalai Lama consulted a possessed oracle in 1959, and that some Southern Baptist and Pentecostal Christians believe in spirit possession. They note that missionaries still oppose voodoo as devil worship.

segments.title: Listener mail: Guantanamo and extraordinary rendition
segments.summary: Listener Will H. writes about a man he met, an Australian Guantanamo detainee who was tortured in Egypt under extraordinary rendition and was drugged so that the torture was ineffective. The hosts discuss a call for voodoo practitioners to write in.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts ask for voodoo practitioners to write in, mention social media and the email address, and sign off.
